title: SKU stability under dynamic context resize and quantization
content:
Summary:
This is a working write-up of experiments comparing A100 / H100 / L40S across multiple cloud SKUs and CUDA/driver combinations, focused on how runtime throughput and tail latency behave when we dynamically resize the effective context window (i.e., we change active KV cache footprint mid-run) and when quantization levels are applied. Goal: identify SKU-driver combinations that are brittle to context-resize events and quantify the HBM spillover/CPU fallback behaviour that leads to tail spikes.

Why this matters (motivation):
- In production we often stitch requests using cache reuse (prefixing) and occasionally must resize or evict KV cache entries (client-initiated context shrink/expand).
- Some GPU SKUs surface large tail-latency regressions when memory pressure triggers HBM->host transfers or when allocation/deallocation happens with different CUDA/driver combos.
- Quantization (int8/4bit) interacts with memory layout and kernel selection; changing the context can flip a different kernel path and cause jitter.

Quick takeaways (draft):
- H100 (p5, p5dn type skus) is robust for steady-state large-context workloads but shows a distinct p99 spike when context resize causes fragmented allocations under CUDA 12.2 drivers.
- A100 is more predictable on older drivers (CUDA 11.8), but on some cloud images the driver's ML cache policy causes short-lived HBM pressure and modest tail increases (~15–25% p99 latency).
- L40S (where available) has the best steady throughput for quantized medium-length contexts, but its driver packaging on some vendors pushes allocation overhead into the host and causes >2x p99 jumps during concurrent resizes.

Test matrix (summary form):
- Models: eval-7B (decoder-only), eval-30B (decoder-only), eval-70B (for memory-starvation edge cases)
- Context lengths: 512, 2048, 8192, 16384 (we simulate resize by starting with 8192 then shrinking/expanding mid-run)
- Batching: batch sizes 1, 4, 8 (focus on tiny-batch microbursts)
- SKUs & infra (representative):
  - AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100, multi-node NVLink)
  - AWS p5.24xlarge (H100, NVLink)
  - GCP a2-highgpu-1g / a2-megagpu (A100)
  - GCP l4d / custom L40S node images (where available)
  - Azure NDv4 / ND H100 variants (spot checks)
- Driver/CUDA combos: CUDA 11.8 + driver X.Y, CUDA 12.1, CUDA 12.2/12.3 (we picked cloud images that claim compatibility), and recent vendor kernel patches (e.g., NVidia driver 530+ vs 545+ in our infra)
- Quantization modes: float32, fp16, int8 (PTQ-like), 4-bit GPTQ-permutations (where supported by runtime)

Methodology (how we ran it - rough):
1) Boot single-tenant instance with chosen SKU and image; pin CPU governor to performance; disable unrelated services.
2) Deploy a minimal serving runtime binary with debug counters and allocation tracing compiled in.
3) Warmup with a steady stream 10k tokens at target context to prime allocators and kernel selection.
4) Run a 30-minute scenario made of: steady-state 10 minutes, then 1 minute where we issue a mid-sequence context-shrink (evict 6k tokens worth of KV), then 5 minutes steady, then expand back to original context, then 10 minutes steady. Repeat for each quant mode and batch size.
5) Collect: token throughput, p50/p90/p95/p99 latencies, GPU memory high-water marks, host page fault counters, NVTX traces (where possible), and runtime allocation logs (lightweight).
6) Repeat each experiment 3x and retain median run.

Representative commands (dev scratch):
- ./serve_infra --model eval-7B --context 8192 --batch 4 --quant fp16 --trace-alloc=alloc-log.json --nvtx
- python tools/context_resizer.py --pid $SERVE_PID --shrink 6000 --delay_ms 1000

Key observations (detailed):
1) HBM fragmentation after repeated resizes
   - On H100 with CUDA 12.2 we saw allocation failures inside the runtime allocator being handled by a slow fallback path that re-allocates and copies in several small chunks. This produced p99 spikes ~3–5x larger than steady-state for ~250–800ms windows after a resize event.
   - The NVidia driver reporting (nvidia-smi) did not always show a short-term memory spike; instead host-side paging counters increased (suggests transient host-touch behaviour within the vendor driver).

2) Quantization kernel path flips
   - In several cases int8 kernels for A100 were selected for steady contexts but for certain resized footprints the runtime chose a different GEMM kernel (presumably due to internal heuristics) which slowed per-token time by ~10–30% for a short window.
   - L40S had the most aggressive kernel switching; combined with some cloud vendor driver packaging it led to CPU interrupts and temporary throughput collapse in concurrent client scenarios.

3) Cloud SKU packaging differences
   - Some cloud images include vendor-managed driver overlays that update kernel module parameters at boot. These overlays sometimes enable stricter numa/cgroups defaults that change allocation behaviour compared to our custom images. Result: identical hardware + different image => measurable p99 delta.

4) Warmup behaviour matters
   - If the steady-state warmup is omitted, the first resize degrades more severely (higher p95/p99). Warmup primes both allocator and kernel selection. Short warmups (2–3k tokens) reduce spike amplitude.

Example micro-results (median of 3 runs, eval-7B, batch=4, quant=fp16):
- p4d (A100, CUDA 11.8): steady throughput 18.2 tokens/s per GPU, p99 baseline 95ms, p99 after resize spike 115ms (+21%).
- p5 (H100, CUDA 12.2): steady throughput 26.1 tokens/s per GPU, p99 baseline 72ms, p99 after resize spike 340ms (+372%).
- L40S (GCP image L40S-2024): steady throughput 28.7 tokens/s, p99 baseline 88ms, p99 after resize spike 210ms (+138%).
(Notes: numbers are synthetic but reflect relative ordering we observed across repeated runs.)

Interpretation / root causes (working hypotheses):
- Driver and CUDA version shape which kernels get chosen, and they also change the allocator/driver fallback behaviour when HBM cannot satisfy reallocations. Newer CUDA/driver stacks appear to enable kernel variants that are faster steady-state but allocate in ways that make fragmentation after resizes worse.
- Cloud image packaging (driver overlays, module options) matter more than we expected. We need a consistent baseline image for replication.
- Quantization reduces memory pressure in steady state but increases sensitivity to small layout changes because packing/stride assumptions differ between int8 kernels — leading to kernel-path thrashing on resize.

Actionable follow-ups (next steps):
- Create a minimal, vendor-agnostic test image with pinned driver versions (11.8, 12.1, 12.2) and a documented boot recipe. Put it in infra/bench-images and use it for a second run.
- Add a lightweight allocation coalescing pass in the runtime to reduce fragmentation on shrink/expand; prototype in a feature branch and bench.
- Add runtime flag to 'delay-evict' KV entries (grace period) to avoid immediate dealloc churn during concurrent threads. Evaluate p99 impact.
- For customer guidance: recommend warmup sequences for large-context workloads and a list of "recommended images" with tested driver combos.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- Need to capture more NVLink internal counters if available (to see whether cross-GPU allocations are affected).
- Re-run with eval-30B and 70B on single large node (p4d multi-gpu) to observe multi-GPU eviction patterns.
- Check kernel logs for page-in/out spikes correlated to our measured p99 windows; file a bug with vendor if host paging is observed.

Replication notes (for engineers):
- Use bench/recipes/sku_context_resize.yml to reproduce; beware cloud image drift (snapshot images by commit).
- Logger level: INFO + allocation trace for resize windows only. Full allocation tracing crashes in large models due to log volume.

Attachments & traces: stored in shared bucket with prefix: gs://redwood-infra/bench-traces/sku-context-resize/2025-02-28/; raw NVTX and alloc logs under run-[sku]-[date].tar.gz

Status / request for review:
- This is a working doc. I need runtime eng and SRE to sanity-check the suggested mitigation (delay-evict) and infra to help produce a reproducible pinned-image. Please review the methodology and point out any blind spots.

Notes to self (scrappy):
- Observed weirdness with nvidia-smi sample interval — use vendor-specific perf counters instead.
- Save a diff of kernel selection logs for the exact token where path flip occurs.
